options.D: Send each breaking response to a second model call that rewrites it into the correct shape

architect-foundations-mock2-8.rationale: Declaring the shape as a schema makes it a contract the model must satisfy, and validation on receipt catches what remains. Examples (A) and repair regexes (B) leave conformity to chance, and a second rewriting call (D) doubles the cost and can introduce its own errors without guaranteeing the schema.
architect-foundations-mock2-8.evidence: Structured outputs constrain generation to a supplied JSON schema; strict tool use guarantees tool inputs match their input_schema.

architect-foundations-mock2-9.task: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
architect-foundations-mock2-9.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. A resume-parsing schema has a string field graduation_year. For 15% of candidates the document has none. Analytics cannot tell "not stated" from "extraction failed" because absent values arrive as empty strings or omitted keys. How should the schema handle this?

options.A: Omit the key whenever the document has no value, and treat any missing key as not stated
options.B: Default to the current year so the field is always populated and the loader needs no null handling
options.C: Return an empty string for absent values and add a separate boolean flagging extraction failures
options.D: Make it nullable so a gap is null, reserving validation errors for failures

architect-foundations-mock2-9.rationale: An explicit nullable representation makes absence a first-class, unambiguous value, while validation errors stay reserved for failures. Omitting keys (A) leaves absence and failure indistinguishable, and a plausible default (B) fabricates data. An empty string plus a flag (C) overloads a text value with two meanings and adds a field to keep in sync.
architect-foundations-mock2-9.evidence: Make fields optional or nullable when the source may lack the information, so the model returns null instead of fabricating a value.

architect-foundations-mock2-10.task: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
architect-foundations-mock2-10.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. A date-and-amount extractor scores 96% on US-format invoices but 71% on European ones, which use 1.234,56 and day-first dates. Failures return the wrong magnitude or swap day and month. What is the most effective response?

options.A: Move to the next larger model tier and re-run the evaluation on the failing subset of invoices
options.B: Add a sentence telling the model to be especially careful with regional number and date formats
options.C: Add European-format examples plus a stated rule for ambiguous or missing values
options.D: Add a pre-processor that rewrites every number into US format before the model reads the text

architect-foundations-mock2-10.rationale: The failures come from formats the prompt never specified, so examples of those formats together with an explicit rule for ambiguity close the gap directly. A bigger model (A) is not aimed at the specification gap, and a generic caution (B) adds no information. A regex pre-processor (D) is brittle over-engineering that can corrupt valid text.
architect-foundations-mock2-10.evidence: Few-shot examples of varied formats and explicit handling of ambiguous or missing values improve consistency on inputs the base prompt did not cover.

architect-foundations-mock2-11.task: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
architect-foundations-mock2-11.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Over two weeks, 14% of tickets show the agent calling search_kb on order-status questions, which it cannot answer, before it eventually calls lookup_order. Both tools have one-line descriptions. A teammate proposes adding a system-prompt paragraph explaining which to use. Which reading of the evidence is correct?

options.A: The catalog is too large, and any tool surface above five tools should be consolidated into one general tool
options.B: Repeated selection of a tool that cannot satisfy the request means the descriptions do not separate the tools, so the interface needs rework
options.C: Order-status questions are a rare edge case, so a routing rule in the system prompt is a proportionate fix
options.D: The tools sit in separate services, and latency differences are skewing the model's choice toward search_kb

architect-foundations-mock2-11.rationale: Tools are selected from their descriptions, so a repeated wrong choice means the descriptions fail to state what each tool does, accepts and is not for. Fixing that at the interface is the root-cause fix. A tool count (A) is not a fault in itself, and a prompt patch for one query type (C) leaves the ambiguity in place. Where services run (D) is not visible to the model.
architect-foundations-mock2-11.evidence: Tool descriptions are the primary signal for tool selection; clear boundaries and when-to-use guidance reduce misrouting among similar tools.

architect-foundations-mock2-12.task: Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
architect-foundations-mock2-12.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An internal ops MCP server exposes delete_record. Its description says "Use with caution; confirm with the user first," yet the agent deleted three staging records without confirmation last week. How should the tool be constrained?

options.A: Enforce authorization and scope in the server and add an approval gate outside the model before the call proceeds
options.B: Rewrite the description with explicit examples of when deletion is and is not acceptable, keeping the warning first
options.C: Add required reason and ticket_id parameters so the model has to justify each deletion call
options.D: Register delete_record last in the tool list so it is less likely to be chosen by the model

architect-foundations-mock2-12.rationale: A description is a request to the model, not a control; limiting a destructive capability requires authorization, scope and approval enforced by the server or harness. Better description wording (B) and extra parameters (C) still rely on the model deciding to comply, since it can fill any value. Tool ordering (D) has no effect on what the tool is allowed to do.
architect-foundations-mock2-12.evidence: Permissions, scoped credentials and approval prompts enforced outside the model bound what a tool can do; descriptions only guide selection.

architect-foundations-mock2-13.task: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
architect-foundations-mock2-13.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A team exposes its customer database to an agent through one MCP tool, run_sql(query), backed by a read-write service account. A security review flags the design. What is the architectural concern?

options.A: The agent inherits the service account's full reach, so scoped tools with narrow credentials are needed for least privilege
options.B: Free-form SQL uses more tokens per call than purpose-built tools, so cost will grow steadily with usage over time
options.C: A single general tool cannot return structured output, so every result has to be parsed back out of text
options.D: Query latency grows with table size, so the agent will time out on the largest tables in the database

architect-foundations-mock2-13.rationale: One unrestricted query tool gives the model whatever authority the credential holds, so nothing can be scoped to the task at hand; several narrow tools with minimal credentials restore least privilege. Token use (B) and latency (D) are secondary operational concerns, and structured output (C) is achievable with either design.
architect-foundations-mock2-13.evidence: Design tools around scoped, well-defined operations and apply least-privilege credentials rather than exposing a general-purpose query surface.

architect-foundations-mock2-14.task: Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration
architect-foundations-mock2-14.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An agent migrating a repository makes about 300 tool calls. Early on it follows the migration conventions, but after call ~200 it re-reads files it already changed and violates decisions it made earlier. Tool latency and model version are unchanged. What is the likely cause?

options.A: The tools have become less reliable over a long session and now return stale data that the model keeps trusting
options.B: Accumulated tool output has diluted the decisions and constraints that matter; persist and re-surface them
options.C: The effort setting is too low for long runs, so the model stops reasoning about earlier decisions
options.D: The prompt cache expired, which removed the earlier decisions from the conversation history

architect-foundations-mock2-14.rationale: Gradual degradation over a long run, with repeated reads and forgotten decisions, is the signature of context accumulation; the remedy is to record decisions in a scratchpad or summary and keep bulky outputs out of the window. Stale tool data (A) would not make the agent contradict its own decisions, and cache expiry (D) affects cost, not the contents of the conversation. Effort (C) does not control what stays salient.
architect-foundations-mock2-14.evidence: Long agent runs accumulate tool output that crowds out earlier decisions; persist key findings externally and summarize to keep context focused.

architect-foundations-mock2-15.task: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
architect-foundations-mock2-15.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. During a four-hour refactor, Claude Code's context was compacted twice. Afterward it reintroduced a pattern the team had banned an hour earlier. What should the workflow do so such constraints survive compaction?

options.A: Rely on the model to keep what matters, since it decides what to retain when it summarizes the session
options.B: Enable the 1M-token context so that compaction never triggers during a refactor of this size and length
options.C: Write the decisions and bans into CLAUDE.md or a notes file that reloads after compaction
options.D: Restart after each compaction and paste the original task description in again

architect-foundations-mock2-15.rationale: Compaction is lossy, so anything that must persist should be written to a durable place the session reloads, such as CLAUDE.md or a notes file. Trusting the summary (A) is unreliable for specific constraints, and a larger window (B) only postpones the boundary. Restarting with the original prompt (D) discards decisions made since the task began.
architect-foundations-mock2-15.evidence: Compaction summarizes the conversation and can lose detail; persistent instructions belong in CLAUDE.md, which is reloaded after compaction.

architect-foundations-mock3-1.task: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
architect-foundations-mock3-1.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Traces show a research agent calling fetch_financial_filings(ticker="ACME") nine times with identical arguments in one task, each call taking about 20 seconds. What does this point to?

options.A: Normal retry behavior that should stay in place, since each call may return fresher data
options.B: A slow tool, so swap in a faster data provider before looking at the agent's behavior at all
options.C: Lost state: the earlier result is not retained, so cache it and surface it in context
options.D: An overeager model, so moving to a smaller tier will cut down redundant exploration

architect-foundations-mock3-1.rationale: Repeating an identical call means the result from the first call is not available to the agent when it decides again, which is a state and context problem solved by caching or persisting results. Retries (A) are for failures, not successful calls, and tool speed (B) does not explain repetition. A smaller model (D) would not change what the agent can see.
architect-foundations-mock3-1.evidence: Agents repeat work when intermediate results are not retained; persist findings and pass them forward rather than re-fetching them.

architect-foundations-mock3-2.task: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
architect-foundations-mock3-2.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are designing an assistant that triages 5,000-line stack traces and also drafts a short user-facing fix summary. A colleague wants a separate subagent for every pair of tasks. What criterion should decide whether two lines of work get separate subagents?

options.A: Whether the work of one would fill the other's context with material it does not need
options.B: Whether the combined prompts would exceed a fixed token threshold regardless of content
options.C: Whether the two lines of work use different tools, since an agent should hold one tool type
options.D: Whether the outputs of the two lines of work will be shown to different end users

architect-foundations-mock3-2.rationale: Subagents exist to isolate context: the trace triage would flood the summary writer's window with noise it does not need, so they should be separate. A fixed token threshold (B) ignores what the content is, and a tool-type rule (C) is not a reason on its own since one agent can hold several tools. The audience for outputs (D) has no bearing on context.
architect-foundations-mock3-2.evidence: Subagents isolate noisy exploration in their own context and return condensed results to the lead agent.

architect-foundations-mock3-3.task: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
architect-foundations-mock3-3.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The agent's bulk-credit tool applies credits to up to 200 accounts at once. Its error rate is low (0.4%), but each error costs about $9,000 to unwind. Which design most reduces the cost of a wrong decision?

options.A: Move to the strongest model tier to push the 0.4% error rate lower still
options.B: Extend the system prompt with a checklist the agent must complete before calling the tool
options.C: Add a read-only preview tool so the agent can check the affected accounts before it commits
options.D: Hold bulk calls for human confirmation, or make credits reversible

architect-foundations-mock3-3.rationale: The risk here is the size of a rare error, so the design should bound the consequence: a confirmation gate or a reversible hold limits what a wrong call can cost. A stronger model (A), a prompt checklist (B) and a self-check preview (C) all aim at the error rate, and none stops a mistaken call from executing.
architect-foundations-mock3-3.evidence: For irreversible or high-impact actions, gate execution behind human approval or make it reversible, enforced outside the model.

architect-foundations-mock3-4.task: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
architect-foundations-mock3-4.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A monorepo's root CLAUDE.md has grown to 3,200 lines over two years and includes notes on retired services. Engineers report Claude Code increasingly ignores rules such as the logging format, even though they are in the file. What is the likely effect, and the fix?

options.A: Longer files give richer context, so the ignored rule should be reworded more forcefully
options.B: The rules that matter compete with stale material, so prune it and move area-specific guidance into path-scoped rules files
options.C: CLAUDE.md is read once at startup and cached, so the logging rule must be restated in each prompt
options.D: Large instruction files slow down every response, so move the content to a wiki outside the repo

architect-foundations-mock3-4.rationale: Project memory is context and dilutes like any other: obsolete material competes with the instructions that matter. Pruning and splitting area-specific guidance into path-scoped rules loads each convention only where it applies. More text (A) is not better context, and repeating the rule in every prompt (C) treats a symptom. Moving everything to a wiki (D) removes the conventions from Claude's context altogether.
architect-foundations-mock3-4.evidence: Keep CLAUDE.md concise and specific; use path-scoped .claude/rules files so conventions load only for matching files.

architect-foundations-mock3-5.task: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
architect-foundations-mock3-5.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A senior engineer proposes committing a deploy-hotfix skill to the shared repository. What should reviewers check before approving it?

options.A: That it is long enough to cover every edge case seen in past hotfix incidents, with each case written out
options.B: That it encodes a procedure the team really repeats, with steps reviewable like ordinary code
options.C: That it is the work of the on-call lead, so the steps reflect real production experience
options.D: That it embeds the full runbook inline so Claude never has to load a supporting file or script

architect-foundations-mock3-5.rationale: A shared skill is justified by a procedure the team genuinely repeats, and because it can run commands it should be reviewable like code. Length and exhaustiveness (A) say nothing about whether it is needed or safe, and authorship (C) is not a control. Inlining everything (D) works against the way skills load supporting files on demand.
architect-foundations-mock3-5.evidence: Skills package repeatable procedures with a SKILL.md and optional supporting files, loaded on demand; shared ones go through normal code review.

architect-foundations-mock3-6.task: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
architect-foundations-mock3-6.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code in CI follows the team's test-naming conventions on some runs and not others, and local results vary by developer. The conventions live in individual engineers' ~/.claude files. Why is committed configuration the better home?

options.A: It loads faster at session start, because it is read from the working directory
options.B: It uses less context, since project files are summarized automatically before they load
options.C: It cannot be overridden, so no developer can diverge from the convention locally
options.D: It is versioned, reviewed with the code, and present in every checkout

architect-foundations-mock3-6.rationale: Committed configuration is part of the repository, so the CI runner checks it out along with the code, and every change to a convention goes through review and history. Load speed (A) and context size (B) are not the reason, and project files are not summarized on load. Local files can still override shared settings (C).
architect-foundations-mock3-6.evidence: Project-level CLAUDE.md and .claude settings are committed to the repository and so apply to every checkout, including automated runs.

architect-foundations-mock3-7.task: Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
architect-foundations-mock3-7.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. About 1 in 400 extraction responses fails schema validation, and the loader currently ingests them anyway after logging a warning. Last month three malformed records reached billing. What is the correct handling?

options.A: Add a fallback path: retry with the validation error, then route to a review queue rather than passing invalid data on
options.B: Accept the rate, since 99.75% valid is within normal tolerance, and keep logging warnings
options.C: Relax strict validation on the fields that fail most, since those rejections are mostly formatting
options.D: Raise max_tokens on every call so that no response can be truncated in the middle of an object

architect-foundations-mock3-7.rationale: A rare failure still needs a defined path: retry with the error message, and if that fails, stop the bad record at a review queue instead of letting it contaminate billing. Tolerating the rate (B) and relaxing validation (C) are the very behaviors that let bad records through. A larger token limit (D) addresses one possible cause only and gives no handling for failures that remain.
architect-foundations-mock3-7.evidence: Validate output against the schema, retry with the specific validation error, and escalate failures rather than passing invalid data downstream.

architect-foundations-mock3-8.task: Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
architect-foundations-mock3-8.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. An extraction service validates output only inside the data warehouse's nightly load, a day after the model call. Bad records have already fed two downstream reports. Why validate right after the model call instead?

options.A: It costs less compute than running the same validation a day later inside the warehouse load job
options.B: It removes the need for a schema, since the validator can infer the expected shape from past outputs
options.C: A failure is caught while it can still be retried or rejected, before later steps use it
options.D: It improves the model's accuracy on later calls, since validation results are learned across requests

architect-foundations-mock3-8.rationale: Validating at the boundary contains a fault at the point where the original document and the model are still available for a retry, and before anything downstream consumes it. Compute cost (A) is incidental, and a validator needs a declared schema to work (B). The model does not learn from validation results across requests (D).
architect-foundations-mock3-8.evidence: Validate extraction output immediately and retry with specific feedback; errors caught at the boundary do not propagate to downstream systems.

architect-foundations-mock3-9.task: Preserve information provenance and handle uncertainty in multi-source synthesis
architect-foundations-mock3-9.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Auditors require each extracted value, such as total_amount, to cite where in the source it came from (page and quote). The current schema returns values only, and searching for the values in the text afterwards fails whenever formatting differs. What does this require?

options.A: A second extraction pass that asks the model to locate each earlier value in the document
options.B: A longer prompt asking the model to remember page numbers and mention them in its explanation
options.C: A model with a larger context window so the full document stays visible while it produces citations
options.D: A schema pairing each value with a page and quote that the model must populate and validate

architect-foundations-mock3-9.rationale: Anything the output must carry has to be part of the declared shape: pairing each value with page and quote, and validating that the pair is present, captures provenance at extraction time. A second locating pass (A) is ungrounded after the fact, and prose requests (B) are probabilistic. Context size (C) does not create the field.
architect-foundations-mock3-9.evidence: Structured claim-source mappings (source, page, excerpt) preserve provenance through extraction and synthesis.

architect-foundations-mock3-10.task: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
architect-foundations-mock3-10.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The agent has search_orders ("Search orders") and find_orders ("Find customer orders"). Traces show a roughly 50/50 split between them for the same kinds of request, with occasionally different results. What is the fault?

options.A: Duplicated code in the two implementations, which should be refactored into one shared module
options.B: Added latency, since the model reads two near-identical descriptions on every turn
options.C: The model has no reliable basis to choose between them, so merge the tools or state each one's boundary in its description
options.D: Extra token cost from carrying two tools, which tool search and deferred loading would remove

architect-foundations-mock3-10.rationale: The model picks tools from their descriptions, and two near-identical ones give it nothing to decide on, so selection becomes arbitrary. The remedy is one tool, or descriptions that state inputs, scope and when to prefer each. Code duplication (A), latency (B) and token cost (D) are secondary and none explains the split in behavior.
architect-foundations-mock3-10.evidence: Overlapping tools with vague descriptions cause misselection; consolidate them or give each distinct, explicit boundaries.

architect-foundations-mock3-11.task: Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
architect-foundations-mock3-11.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. lookup_order is called with order_id "12345", but the backend expects "ORD-12345". The tool returns an empty list, and the agent tells customers no order exists. What should the tool do instead?

options.A: Return the closest-matching order by fuzzy search so the customer still gets a useful answer
options.B: Return an error that says the ID format is invalid and which pattern the backend expects
options.C: Raise an exception that ends the run and pages an on-call engineer to look at the failing call
options.D: Return an empty list as now, and tell the agent in the prompt to retry with an ORD- prefix

architect-foundations-mock3-11.rationale: A structured error that says what was wrong and what is expected lets the model fix its own call, and keeps a recoverable problem recoverable. A fuzzy guess (A) risks returning the wrong customer's order, and an empty list (D) is indistinguishable from a true no-match, so the agent cannot learn the cause. Ending the run (C) turns a one-token fix into an incident.
architect-foundations-mock3-11.evidence: MCP tools should return errors with isError, an error category and an actionable message so the agent can recover.

architect-foundations-mock3-12.task: Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
architect-foundations-mock3-12.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your read-only code-search workflow connects to a third-party MCP server that also exposes create_issue and delete_branch. Neither is needed for this use case. What should you do?

options.A: Restrict the integration to the read tools with an allowlist or deny rules, so unneeded authority is not granted
options.B: Keep them enabled and rely on the approval prompt, since they may be useful for future workflows that the team plans
options.C: Add a line in CLAUDE.md saying not to call write tools during code-search sessions
options.D: Rename the tools with a deprecated_ prefix so the model is discouraged from selecting them

architect-foundations-mock3-12.rationale: Authority that the use case does not need should not be granted: allowlisting only the read tools removes the write capability instead of discouraging it. Keeping them (B) leaves the capability reachable, and an instruction in CLAUDE.md (C) or a renamed tool (D) only nudges the model while the call remains possible.
architect-foundations-mock3-12.evidence: Permission rules (allow and deny) can limit which MCP tools Claude Code may call; grant only the access the workflow needs.

architect-foundations-mock3-13.task: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
architect-foundations-mock3-13.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A research run lasts about 90 minutes. You want an automated monitor that detects context-management failure as early as possible. Which signal is the most direct?

options.A: The agent starts repeating searches or contradicting earlier findings
options.B: Run duration exceeds the median for comparable topics by more than 50%, measured per task
options.C: Per-run token cost climbs above the previous week's average cost for similar tasks
options.D: A search tool returns an error such as a timeout or a 429 response from the provider

architect-foundations-mock3-13.rationale: Repeated work and self-contradiction are the behavioral signature of lost state, so they point straight at context loss. Longer duration (B) and higher cost (C) rise for many unrelated reasons, such as a larger topic, and a tool error (D) is an integration problem unrelated to what the agent remembers.
architect-foundations-mock3-13.evidence: Repeating earlier work or contradicting earlier decisions in long sessions signals that important context has been lost or diluted.

architect-foundations-mock3-14.task: Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
architect-foundations-mock3-14.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The agent sometimes stops after proposing a refund without issuing it, and sometimes loops on tickets that were already resolved. Nobody has defined what "resolved" means. Why does the system need a defined success criterion?

options.A: It shortens the prompt by replacing the procedural instructions with a single goal statement for the agent
options.B: Without one, completion can't be told from failure, so it can't stop or be measured
options.C: It lowers token cost by capping the number of tool calls an agent may make in a single run
options.D: The Agent SDK requires one to be set before an agent loop will start running at all, by design

architect-foundations-mock3-14.rationale: Termination and measurement both depend on a definition of done: without it the agent stops early or loops, and evaluation has no target for first-contact resolution. Prompt length (A) and call caps (C) are side effects at best, and the SDK has no such requirement (D).
architect-foundations-mock3-14.evidence: Define explicit completion and escalation criteria so the agent knows when a task is resolved, and so resolution can be measured.

architect-foundations-mock3-15.task: Design human review workflows and confidence calibration
architect-foundations-mock3-15.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Compliance says an incorrect extracted dosage must never reach the pharmacist's screen unnoticed. Current accuracy on the evaluation set is 98.5%. What does the design need?

options.A: Move to the most capable model tier to raise accuracy above 99.5% on the evaluation set
options.B: Add ten more few-shot examples covering unusual dosage notations, units and abbreviations from the feed
options.C: A detection step, such as cross-field checks or a verifier, plus a defined action when it fires, like human review
options.D: Extend the context window so the full prescription history is visible on every call

architect-foundations-mock3-15.rationale: A requirement about errors not going unnoticed is a detection-and-response requirement: a check that flags suspect records, plus a defined action such as routing to review. A stronger model (A), more examples (B) and more context (D) raise average accuracy, but none catches the individual bad output.
architect-foundations-mock3-15.evidence: Route low-confidence or failed-validation extractions to human review; accuracy gains alone do not catch individual errors.
